City of Lights is a true crime podcast that tells the truth

Willy Nast’s podcast—which centers on the unsolved murder of Chicagoland teen Jeff Signorelli—feels distinct within a crowded genre.
by Katie Prout August 31, 2026August 31, 2026

Instaread

Often, in true crime stories, there’s a narrative urge to make something of the terrible experience endured by the people at the story’s heart. As the reader (or listener, in the case of podcasts), we can’t help but hope for catharsis; if the life can’t be saved, the child found, or the murder solved, we’ll settle for the relief of believing that grief doesn’t just grind on, endless and unchanged, for the victim’s loved ones. We want to hear that they turned their pain into productivity, that old American vice, maybe by passing a law or founding a nonprofit. In other words, by the end of the story, we want these people to be relatively OK, because if they are, it’s easier to pretend that, in their shoes, we’d be OK, too. 

City of Lights, the first podcast of writer Willy Nast, flips this script on its head. It’s ostensibly a true crime tale about the unsolved murder of Jeff Signorelli, a teenager from Aurora, Illinois, who was shot in July 2002—the summer after he finished high school, on the humid cusp of the rest of his life. But City of Lights doesn’t prioritize the comfort of the listener or force the story into a tidy narrative arc. Instead, Nast does something different: He tells the truth. 

In the first of six episodes, Nast lets the listener know that this isn’t a whodunnit: Jeff’s murder remains unsolved. Instead, the question this podcast asks is, “What now?” To provoke interest in that question, Nast uses his creative nonfiction background and shoe-leather journalism to introduce listeners to the physical and emotional topography of this story, and to reconstruct the last day of Jeff’s life. In the middle of “a bad week, in a bad month, in a bad year,” in which Aurora was reeling from frequent gun violence, a young man woke up for the last time and put on his uniform for his crappy but fun summer job at a local water park. Perhaps, Nast says, Jeff pet his cat, Zeke; he grabbed a thermos of earl grey tea from his mom. On his way to work, he listened to the loud, angry music favored by many teenage white boys of the early aughts—maybe Korn, maybe Limp Bizkit—though, Nast tells us, Jeff was neither loud nor angry. “He was alive.”

This tenderness and attention to detail permeates the rest of the podcast. Nast himself is a character in this series, though one on the side, and he is clear with the listener about why he made that craft decision from jump. Makers of literary journalism endlessly debate the wisdom of including or excluding the narrative “I” in their work. Nast touches on this, in the first and last episodes; by the series end, he’s gone from the side of Truman Capote to the side of Janet Malcolm. (If you don’t know what that means, listen anyway—it’s good.) 

The snippets of Nast’s life as he grows and matures contrast quietly but sharply with the shortness of Jeff’s life. But the name of the podcast isn’t Willy, and it isn’t Jeff. It isn’t Mary Ann and Al, Jeff’s parents, though the focus of the story is clearly on the couple, with a particular care for Mary Ann, Jeff’s fierce, funny, and bleak mother. It’s City of Lights, one of Aurora’s nicknames. Nast rightly treats the city of Aurora as a character in this story and turns his ruthlessly focused midwestern politesse to the behavior of Aurora’s politicians—mayors, alderpeople, and state representatives—and the bureaucratic systems they uphold. There is a delicious moment when, while ever persistent and polite, Nast uses archival records of a politician’s own words to catch them in a lie. In this way, City of Lights fits well within the broader landscape of Chicagoland podcasts popping up over the last few years, many of which cover youth death, violence, the systems and politicians at fault, and the survivors who try, in the aftermath of their loss, to make sense and make change: Motive from WBEZ, Somebody and You Didn’t See Nothin, both from the Invisible Institute.

City of Lights
Six hour-long episodes

Attention can be cruel—especially the gawking attention of fans of the true crime genre—but it also can be an act of compassion. Nast, who now lives in Iowa but who spent decades in Chicago, grew up in Aurora and knew Jeff, though they weren’t close. In 2008, he began interviewing Mary Ann and Al Signorelli for his undergraduate thesis at Northwestern University; he hoped to turn their interviews into a book. Eighteen years later, City of Lights was released instead. “Wouldn’t it be funny if I was still working on this when I’m 30?” he jokes during an interview in one episode. Later, breaking into the tape from the present, Nast notes that he has two kids and is now 42. This story benefits immensely from the maturity that time brings. The penultimate episode walks through the night that Jeff died. A difficult listen, this episode is where I personally felt certain that turning this story into a podcast, rather than a book, was the right move. As listeners, we are carried by the strength of hearing their voices and the silence around some of their more devastating words. Mary Ann and Al were obliterated by their only child’s death, and Nast lets us sit in the aftermath of that obliteration. Sometimes, there is nothing more to say.

There is one last episode, though. You’ll need to listen to the whole season to appreciate the ending, which I won’t spoil here, but by the end of the podcast, Al and Mary Ann—nearly 20 years after the unsolved murder of their only child—are not the kind of people who say it gets better. In fact, Mary Ann herself will tell you that you don’t even have to survive grief, if you don’t want to; there is a brief, direct, terrible minute in which she tells Nast she understands why, in the aftermath of great loss, some people choose suicide. She didn’t. Instead, Mary Ann and Al try mightily but do not succeed at any of the initiatives to address gun violence that they start in the aftermath of Jeff’s death. There is no grand triumph over grief here. There is no catharsis; they do not Make Something Of It. Via a small, unexpected twist at the end, Nast shows the couple’s real legacy: There is dignity in just surviving alongside your loss and still engaging in the world with curiosity and care.

Listen if you like: local news; library microfiche; regional accents; dignity; midwesterners who don’t swear unless they’re really, really mad; and a surprise mention of Rod Blagojevich.

Katie Prout

Katie Prout (she/her/hers) is a features writer for the Chicago Reader. She received her BA from Kalamazoo College and her MFA in Nonfiction from the University of Iowa.

In 2020, Katie’s profile of Chicago blues artist Mary Lane was anthologized in Dispatches from the Rust Belt: Volume III. In 2023, her reported essay on her struggle to find a psychiatrist who accepts Medicaid was included in the anthology Going for Broke: Living on the Edge in the World’s Richest Country. Currently, she's working on a book about the intersection of the overdose crisis and homelessness in Chicago, via the lens of her own family's experience with addiction and economic precarity, called Life and Death in the Loop. kprout@chicagoreader.com
